name: describe_schema
description:
Returns the columns, keys, and indexes of relations `search_schema` found.
Run this after `search_schema`, naming at most 20 tables per call, each written
as `schema.table` or as a bare `table`. Every relation comes back with its
columns, its primary key, its foreign keys, and its indexes. A relation marked
`truncated` had metadata left out by a bound or by the database privileges the
read-only role holds: what is present is accurate, but it is not everything.

tables.description: Tables to describe, as `schema.table` or a bare `table`; at most 20 per call.

ColumnDetail.description: One column of a discovered relation.

comment.description: The bounded column comment, when one exists.

default.description: The bounded column default, when one exists.

name.description: The constraint name, when the engine reports one.

referenced_columns.description: The referenced columns, positionally aligned with `columns`.

IndexSummary.description: An index on a discovered relation.

primary.description: Whether the index backs the primary key.

SchemaSummary.description: One schema and the relations the role may see.

foreign_keys.description: Foreign keys declared on this relation.

kind.description: What kind of relation it is.

primary_key.description: Primary-key column names, in key order.

truncated.description:
Whether any of this relation's metadata was left out.

Set when a bound cuts a list or catalog text, when an engine reports a key part
without a column name, and when a foreign-key target is hidden by policy or
database privileges. Warden omits unavailable metadata rather than inventing or
exposing it, and says the result is partial.

WireTableKind.description:
What kind of relation a discovered object is, as a closed wire enum.

Mirrors [`TableKind`]'s variant names exactly, so its own
`#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]` reproduces `TableKind`'s spelling by
construction rather than by a hand-copied match arm that could drift from it. The
core enum has no `Display` to delegate to instead.

name: explain
description:
Returns the engine's plan for a statement without executing it.
The statement is planned, never run. Every policy `query` applies is applied
here too, because planning is real work on the server rather than a dry run.
The plan is the engine's own document: its costs are that engine's units, and
they are not comparable between dialects.

connection.description: The connection to plan against; determines the dialect and placeholder syntax.

parameters.description: Values bound to the statement's placeholders, in the statement's own order.

items.description: One placeholder value. Containers are not accepted: pass a scalar per placeholder in the statement's own order.

sql.description: The statement to plan. Never executed.

PlanSummaryOutput.description:
The engine-independent part of a plan.

There is no cost field, for the same reason `warden-core`'s own [`PlanSummary`] has
none: MySQL and PostgreSQL cost units are not comparable (`docs/architecture.md`
section 11).

estimated_rows.description:
The planner's row estimate, when it reports one.

PostgreSQL fills this; MySQL leaves it `null` rather than borrowing one of its
own per-step estimates, which would be Warden stating a number the server never
stated (`docs/architecture.md` section 11; `docs/open-questions.md` item 20).

WireDialect.description:
The dialect, as a closed wire enum rather than an open `String`.

[`Dialect`] is a closed set, so the derived schema can state the two legal values
(`docs/mcp.md` section 1.2 treats the derived schema as a verifiable contract, not
prose) instead of an unconstrained string a client cannot validate against. The
variant names are chosen so `#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]` reproduces
`Dialect`'s own `#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]` spelling exactly: `Mysql` has no
internal case transition, so snake_case lowers it to `"mysql"`, matching
`Dialect::as_str()`; likewise `Postgresql` to `"postgresql"`.

dialect.description: The dialect that produced the plan.

plan.description: The engine's own plan document, passed through unchanged.

name: list_connections
description:
Lists the connections this server can reach, with the dialect each one speaks.
Call this first. The connection you pick decides which SQL dialect the `query`
and `explain` tools accept and which placeholder syntax they take: `?` on MySQL
and `$1` on PostgreSQL. The response carries public metadata only — never a
host, a user, or a connection string.

ConnectionSummary.description:
One configured connection.

No field a DSN could hide in: this mirrors [`ConnectionMetadata`], which cannot hold
one either (SPEC section 6, invariant 20).

database.description: The default database or catalog, for the agent's orientation.

environment.description:
The deployment environment, e.g. `"production"`.

A `String`, not a closed wire enum like `dialect`: the core
[`warden_core::connection::Environment`] it comes from has an open
`Other(String)` variant for operator-defined environments, so no closed schema
could represent every legal value.

name.description: The name an agent passes to every tool.

WireDialect.description:
The dialect, as a closed wire enum rather than an open `String`.

[`Dialect`] is a closed set, so the derived schema can state the two legal values
(`docs/mcp.md` section 1.2 treats the derived schema as a verifiable contract, not
prose) instead of an unconstrained string a client cannot validate against. The
variant names are chosen so `#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]` reproduces
`Dialect`'s own `#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]` spelling exactly: `Mysql` has no
internal case transition, so snake_case lowers it to `"mysql"`, matching
`Dialect::as_str()`; likewise `Postgresql` to `"postgresql"`.

connections.description: Every connection this deployment is configured to reach.

name: query
description:
Runs a single read-only `SELECT` and returns the rows it produced.
Only a single `SELECT` is accepted, read-only CTEs included. `INSERT`, `UPDATE`,
`DELETE`, DDL, and several statements in one call are rejected, and so are
`SHOW`, `EXPLAIN`, and `SET`: planning has the `explain` tool, and the other two
are unavailable here. Placeholders are dialect-native — `?` on MySQL, `$1` on
PostgreSQL — with one value per placeholder, in the statement's own order.
Results are bounded: when the response reports `truncated`, refine the statement
— a narrower projection, a filter, a smaller `LIMIT` — rather than repeating it
unchanged.

connection.description:
The configured connection to run against; determines the dialect and
placeholder syntax. See `list_connections`.

parameters.description:
Values bound to the statement's placeholders, in the statement's own order.
Omit for a statement with no placeholders.

items.description: One placeholder value. Containers are not accepted: pass a scalar per placeholder in the statement's own order.

sql.description: The statement to execute, using the connection's own placeholder syntax.

database_type.description: The database type name, preserved so the agent keeps the original meaning.

name.description: The name the database reported, duplicates included.

nullable.description: Nullability, when the driver reports it.

bytes.description: Normalized size of the result in bytes.

duration_ms.description: Wall-clock execution time, in whole milliseconds.

items.description: One normalized cell. An integer outside ±2^53 arrives as a decimal string so no client rounds it; the column's own type is in `columns[i].database_type`.

truncated.description: Whether a limit stopped collection early. Refine the query rather than repeat it.

name: search_schema
description:
Finds relations by name, before you write a statement against them.
Run `search_schema` before `query`: it is how you discover the relation names
this connection actually has. Its `query` argument accepts several free-text
terms in one string, separated by whitespace. Results are bounded and ranked by
how each relation matched, so even a broad search returns the best matches
rather than the whole catalog; narrow the terms when what you need is not among
them. Follow it with `describe_schema` for the columns and keys of the relations
you picked.

limit.description: The largest number of matches to return. Defaults to 20 when omitted.

query.description: Free-text search terms, separated by whitespace.

kind.description: What kind of relation it is.

reason.description:
Why it matched: `"exact_table"`, `"table_prefix"`, `"table_substring"`,
`"column_match"`, `"schema_name"`, or `"description"`, in ranking order.

WireMatchReason.description:
Why a search hit ranked where it did, as a closed wire enum.

Mirrors [`MatchReason`]'s variant names exactly, for the same reason
[`WireTableKind`] mirrors [`TableKind`]'s.

oneOf.description: The table name started with the term.
The table name contained the term.

WireTableKind.description:
What kind of relation a discovered object is, as a closed wire enum.

Mirrors [`TableKind`]'s variant names exactly, so its own
`#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]` reproduces `TableKind`'s spelling by
construction rather than by a hand-copied match arm that could drift from it. The
core enum has no `Display` to delegate to instead.

truncated.description: Whether the limit stopped collection early.
